arXiv:2410.10147v5 [math.PR] 07 Apr 2026
Local Optimality of Dictator Functions with Applications to Courtade–Kumar
and Li–Médard Conjectures
Thanks: Accepted for publication in the Annals of Applied Probability. This extended version includes additional proofs, auxiliary formulas, and comprehensive matlab scripts not present in the published version.
Lei Yu
August 24, 2026
Given a convex function \Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}, the \Phi-stability
of a Boolean function f is defined as \mathbb{E}[\Phi(T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{X}))],
where \mathbf{X} is a random vector uniformly distributed on the
discrete cube \{\pm 1\}^{n} and T_{\rho} is the Bonami-Beckner
operator. In this paper, we prove that dictator functions are locally
optimal in maximizing the \Phi-stability of f over all balanced
Boolean functions. When focusing on the symmetric q-stability,
combining this result with our previous bound, we use computer-assisted
methods to prove that dictator functions maximize the symmetric q-stability
for q=1 and \rho\in[0,0.914] or for q\in[1.36,2) and all
\rho\in[0,1]. In other words, we confirm the (balanced) Courtade–Kumar
conjecture with the correlation coefficient \rho\in[0,0.914] and
the (symmetrized) Li–Médard conjecture with q\in[1.36,2). We
conjecture that dictator functions maximize both the symmetric and
asymmetric \frac{1}{2}-stability over all balanced Boolean functions.
Our proofs are based on majorization of noise operators and hypercontractivity
inequalities.
??School of Statistics and Data Science, LPMC, KLMDASR, and LEBPS,
Nankai University, Tianjin 300071, China , ??
1 Introduction
Let \mathbf{X} be a random vector uniformly distributed on the
discrete cube \{\pm 1\}^{n}. Let \mathbf{Y}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} be
the random vector obtained by independently changing the sign of each
component of \mathbf{X} with the same probability \frac{1-\rho}{2}.
Here, \rho\in[0,1] corresponds to the correlation coefficient between
each component of \mathbf{X} and the corresponding one of \mathbf{Y}.
Let T_{\rho}=T_{\rho}^{(n)} be the noise operator (also known as
the Bonami-Beckner operator) which acts on Boolean functions
f:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} such that T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{Y})|\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}].
Let \Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous and strictly convex
function.
Definition 1.1.
For a Boolean function f:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}, the \Phi-stability
of f with respect to (w.r.t.) correlation coefficient \rho is
defined as
\displaystyle\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{X}))].
The noise stability problem, in a general sense, concerns which Boolean
functions (or measurable sets) are the “most stable” under the
action of the noise operator. In terms of \Phi-stability, the noise
stability problem is formulated as
\max_{f:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\},\mathbb{E}f=\alpha}\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f].
It is known (e.g., in [34]) that
I_{\Phi}(f(\mathbf{Y});\mathbf{X})=\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]-\Phi(\mathbb{E}f),
where I_{\Phi}(f(\mathbf{Y});\mathbf{X}):=\operatorname{Ent}_{\Phi}(f(\mathbf{Y}))-\operatorname{Ent}_{\Phi}(f(\mathbf{Y})|\mathbf{X})
is the \Phi-mutual information between f(\mathbf{Y}) and \mathbf{X}.
Here, \operatorname{Ent}_{\Phi}(f(\mathbf{Y})):=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(f(\mathbf{Y}))]-\Phi(\mathbb{E}f(\mathbf{Y}))
is the \Phi-entropy of f(\mathbf{Y}), and \operatorname{Ent}_{\Phi}(f(\mathbf{Y})|\mathbf{X}):=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(f(\mathbf{Y}))]-\mathbb{E}\Phi(\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{Y})|\mathbf{X}])
is the conditional \Phi-entropy of f(\mathbf{Y}) given
\mathbf{X}. So, maximizing the \Phi-stability w.r.t. volume
\alpha\in[0,1] is equivalent to maximizing the \Phi-mutual information
between f(\mathbf{Y}) and \mathbf{X} over all Boolean functions
with \mathbb{E}f=\alpha; see details in [34].
In the learning languages, the noise stability problem admits a natural interpretation. Let \mathbf{X} denote the data we are truly interested in, and let \mathbf{Y} denote its noisy counterpart—the data actually accessible to us. We aim to learn a single bit of information about \mathbf{X} but only using \mathbf{Y}. A key question then arises: what is the most informative bit about \mathbf{X} that we can extract from \mathbf{Y}? For specific functions \Phi, it was conjectured in the literature that the dictator function is optimal for this purpose. This conjecture is known as the “most informative bit” conjecture, and it will be introduced in detail in the following subsection.
1.1 Related Conjectures
Consider two instances of \Phi. For q>0, define \Phi_{q},\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}
as
\displaystyle\Phi_{q}(t)
\displaystyle:=t\ln_{q}(t)\quad\textrm{ and \quad}\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}(t):=t\ln_{q}(t)+(1-t)\ln_{q}(1-t),
where 0\ln_{q}(0):=0, and the function \ln_{q}:(0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}
is defined as
\ln_{q}(t):=\begin{cases}\frac{t^{q-1}-1}{q-1},&q\neq 1\\
\ln(t),&q=1\end{cases}
and is known as the q-logarithm introduced by Tsallis [32],
but with a slight reparameterization. In particular, for q=1,
we also denote
h(t):=\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}(t)=t\ln t+(1-t)\ln(1-t).
The function -h is known as the binary entropy function.
Definition 1.2.
The \Phi_{q}-stability and the \Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}-stability
are respectively called the asymmetric and symmetric q-stabilities,
denoted as \mathbf{Stab}_{q} and \mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}.
For a Boolean function f, by definition, I_{\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}}(f(\mathbf{Y});\mathbf{X})
reduces to the Tsallis mutual information between f(\mathbf{Y})
and \mathbf{X}. In particular, when q=1, I_{\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}}(f(\mathbf{Y});\mathbf{X})
reduces to the Shannon mutual information (denoted as I(f(\mathbf{Y});\mathbf{X})
for short).
There are several fundamental conjectures on the noise stability.
A Boolean function f_{\mathrm{d}} is called a dictator function
if f_{\mathrm{d}}=1\{x_{k}=1\} or 1\{x_{k}=-1\} for some 1\leq k\leq n.
Conjecture 1.3 (Asymmetric q-Stability Conjecture).
For 0\leq\rho\leq 1 and q\in[1,9],
it holds that \mathbf{Stab}_{q}(f)\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}(f_{\mathrm{d}})
for all balanced Boolean functions f, where f_{\mathrm{d}} is
a dictator function.
Conjecture 1.4 (Symmetric q-Stability Conjecture).
For 0\leq\rho\leq 1 and q\in[1,9],
it holds that \mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}(f)\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}(f_{\mathrm{d}})
for all balanced Boolean functions f, where f_{\mathrm{d}} is
a dictator function.
These two conjectures are unifications of several existing conjectures [34].
These two conjectures are known as the Mossel–O’Donnell
conjecture [24] when q\in(2,9], known as the Li–Médard conjecture [22] when q\in(1,2), and known as the Courtade–Kumar conjecture when q=1.
In particular, for q=1, the Courtade–Kumar
conjecture can be interpreted as the problem of maximizing the Shannon
mutual information I(f(\mathbf{Y});\mathbf{X}) over all Boolean
functions f with a given mean. This conjecture attracts considerable
interest from different fields [2, 18, 27, 30, 28, 22],
and it is regarded as one of the most fundamental conjectures at the
interface of information theory and the analysis of Boolean functions.
Furthermore, it is known that the Courtade–Kumar conjecture is equivalent
to the Li–Médard conjecture [3]. It is
also interesting to ask a stronger question: What is the interval
[a,b]\subset[1,\infty) for which dictator functions maximize asymmetric
(or symmetric) q-stability if and only if q\in[a,b] [34]?
It is known that such an interval exists [3, 37].
Besides the motivation from learning theory given above,
other motivations for studying the noise stability problem are as follows.
Maximizing noise stability for Boolean functions with given mean is
equivalent to minimizing the size of a “soft-boundary” for subsets
with given size. In fact, the classic edge-isoperimetric inequality
proven by Harper can be recovered from the noise stability problem
(by taking the limit \rho\to 1) [20, 10, 22].
So, the noise stability problem can be seen as a probabilistic generalization
of the classic isoperimetric problem. Furthermore, the noise stability
problem can recover the classic hypercontractivity inequality, which
means that the noise stability problem is a strengthening of the hypercontractivity
inequality [25, 21]. The noise
stability problem has also many applications in Boolean function analysis.
By Fourier expansion, the noise stability of a Boolean function is
exactly the generating function of Fourier weights of this Boolean
function, where the correlation coefficient \rho is the indeterminate
[26]. On the other hand, estimating Fourier
weights is a fundamental question in Boolean function analysis.
1.2 Related Works
The study of the noise stability problem, or more precisely, a two-function
(or two-set) version of the noise stability problem called the non-interactive
correlation distillation (NICD) problem, dates back to Gács and Körner’s
and Witsenhausen’s seminal papers [16, 33].
By utilizing the tensorization property of the maximal correlation,
Witsenhausen [33] showed that for q=2,
the asymmetric and symmetric 2-stability w.r.t. \alpha=1/2 are
attained by dictator functions. The symmetric q-stability problem
with q\in\left\{3,4,5,...\right\} was studied by Mossel and O’Donnell
[24], and the case q=3 was solved by them.
Specifically, they showed that for q=3, the symmetric q-stability
w.r.t. \alpha=1/2 is maximized by dictator functions. This result
was improved by the present author in [34] by showing
that the asymmetric and symmetric q-stability w.r.t. \alpha=1/2
are maximized by dictator functions for q\in[2,3] and q\in[2,5]
respectively. As for the other direction, Mossel and O’Donnell observed
that the asymmetric and symmetric q-stability are not maximized
by dictator functions for q=10.
In 2016, Samorodnitsky [30] made a significant
breakthrough on the Courtade–Kumar conjecture. Specifically, he
proved the existence of a dimension-independent threshold
\rho_{0} for which the Courtade–Kumar conjecture holds for all
\rho\in[0,\rho_{0}]. However, the value of \rho_{0} was not
explicitly given in his paper, and required to be “sufficiently
small”. In 2023, the present author [34] used a different
method to prove an explicit threshold \rho_{1}\approx 0.46 for which
the Courtade–Kumar conjecture holds for all \rho\in[0,\rho_{1}].
In addition, the present author also provided a bound for the Courtade–Kumar
conjecture in [34] which is expressed in the form of
finite-dimensional program. By evaluating this bound, numerical results
indicate that the threshold \rho_{1} here can be improved to 0.83.
In addition, Anantharam et al. proposed a strengthened version of the Courtade–Kumar conjecture
by considering another specific \Phi-stability [1],
and Chen and Nair proved bounds for this kind of \Phi-stability
by using ideas from isoperimetric inequalities in [9].
By considering a variant of noise model, Eldan, Mikulincer, and Raghavendra
recently proved a variant version of the Courtade–Kumar conjecture
[13], whose proof is based on the so-called renormalized
Brownian motion. A weaker version (i.e., the two-function version) of Courtade–Kumar
conjecture was solved by Pichler, Piantanida, and Matz [28]
by using Fourier analysis. Specifically, they showed that I(f(\mathbf{Y});g(\mathbf{X}))
is maximized by a pair of identical dictator functions over all Boolean
functions (f,g), not limited to balanced ones.
The \Phi-stability problem in the Gaussian setting with \Phi
restricted to be convex and increasing was fully resolved by Borell
[6] in 1985. In particular, he showed that
the \Phi-stability is maximized by the indicators of half-spaces
over all measurable Boolean functions f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\{0,1\}
of the same measure. Such a result is known as Borell’s Isoperimetric
Theorem. The Gaussian analogues of Conjectures 1.3
and 1.4 with q\in[1,\infty) are implied
by Borell’s Isoperimetric Theorem, which were also proved respectively
by Kindler, O’Donnell, and Witmer [18] and
by Eldan [12] using alternative approaches.
1.3 Our Contributions
Rearrangement and majorization techniques are efficient tools in proving
geometric inequalities. Such techniques were also used in the study
of the noise stability problem [6, 18, 9].
In this paper, we investigate the majorization of T_{\rho}f for
a Boolean function f, and connect it to the noise stability. We
then use the majorization and hypercontractivity inequalities to
provide upper bounds on the \Phi-stability. By these bounds, we
prove that dictator functions locally maximize the \Phi-stability
among all balanced Boolean functions. When focusing on the symmetric
q-stability, combining this result with our previous bound, we
use computer-assisted methods to prove that dictator functions maximize
the symmetric q-stability for q=1 and \rho\in[0,0.914] or
for q\in[1.36,2) and all \rho\in[0,1].
In other words, our main results are the following two theorems.
Theorem 1.5.
The Courtade–Kumar
conjecture is true for all \rho\in[0,0.914].
Theorem 1.6.
The (symmetrized) Li–Médard conjecture is
true for all q\in[1.36,2) and \rho\in[0,1], and also true for all q\in(1,1.36) and \rho\in[0,0.914].
For q\in(1,1.36), we numerically
evaluate our bound and find a region of (q,\rho) for which dictator
functions maximize the q-stability (i.e., for which the Li–Médard
conjecture is true). We plot this region in Fig. 1.
In addition, it is also interesting to consider the case q\in(0,1).
For this case, we conjecture that dictator functions maximize both
the symmetric and asymmetric \frac{1}{2}-stability over all balanced
Boolean functions.
Note Added: After the submission of this work, a related study [8] by Chen, Gohari, and Nair was posted on arXiv in Feb. 2025. In their work, they reduced the Courtade–Kumar conjecture to a set of conjectured inequalities involving up to 4 variables.
Fig 1: The region of (q,\rho) (the gray region here)
for which dictator functions maximize the q-stability (i.e., for
which the Li–Médard conjecture is true). For q=1, the maximum
\rho on the boundary of this region is \rho=0.914. For q\geq 1.36,
the corresponding \rho on the boundary of this region is \rho=1.
1.4 Organization
This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce majorization
theory. In Section 3, we investigate the majorization for noise operators.
In Section 4, we investigate the local optimality of dictator functions
in maximizing the \Phi-stability. In Section 5, we focus on the
q-stability and investigate the global optimality of dictator functions
in maximizing the q-stability. We improve our previous bounds on
the Courtade–Kumar conjecture and the Li–Médard conjecture. In
Section 6, we extend our bounds on the \Phi-stability to arbitrary
Boolean functions and also to the Gaussian setting. The proofs of
our results are provided in Appendices A-H.
2 Preliminaries
Since proofs of our results in this paper rely on majorization, we
introduce basic concepts and properties in this field. Here, we adopt the notations
in [23]. Let (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu)
be a measure space and let f be a nonnegative \mu-integrable
(real-valued) function defined on \mathcal{X}. Define the distribution
function of f with respect to \mu as
\mathfrak{m}_{f}(t):=\mu\{x:f(x)>t\},\;t\geq 0.
(1)
Define the decreasing rearrangement of f as
f_{\downarrow}(v):=\sup\{t:\mathfrak{m}_{f}(t)>v\},\;v\geq 0.
(2)
It is easy to see that the distribution function \mathfrak{m}_{f} is nonincreasing and right-continuous on [0,\infty), and finite on (0,\infty). Moreover,
f_{\downarrow}(v)=\lambda\{t:\mathfrak{m}_{f}(t)>v\}=\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{m}_{f}}(v),\;\forall v\geq 0,
where \lambda is the Lebesgue measure on \mathbb{R}_{+}:=[0,\infty).
Thus, the decreasing rearrangement of f is the distribution function
(w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure \lambda) of the distribution function (w.r.t. the original measure \mu) of f. Furthermore, it should be
noting that the domain of f_{\downarrow} is [0,\mu(\mathcal{X})]
which usually differs from the domain \mathcal{X} of f.
Definition 2.1.
Let f and g be nonnegative integrable functions on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu).
The function f is majorized by g, denoted f\prec g, if
1.
\int_{0}^{t}f_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v\leq\int_{0}^{t}g_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v,\;\forall t\geq 0;
2.
\int f{\rm d}\mu=\int g{\rm d}\mu.
Since \int f{\rm d}\mu=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{f}(t){\rm d}t=\int_{0}^{\infty}f_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v,
the second condition can be rewritten as \int_{0}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{f}(t){\rm d}t=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{g}(t){\rm d}t,
or equivalently, \int_{0}^{\infty}f_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v=\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v.
The quantity \int_{0}^{t}f_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v is in fact closely
related to the optimal tradeoff between two types of errors in hypothesis
testing. Note that
A\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}\mapsto\int_{A}f{\rm d}\mu defines a measure,
which is denoted by \mu_{f}. For a nonnegative
function f, define the concentration spectrum
\displaystyle\mathfrak{D}_{f}(t)
\displaystyle:=\sup_{A:\mu(A)\leq t}\mu_{f}(A).
(3)
and its smooth version
\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{f}(t)
\displaystyle:=\sup_{\phi:\mu(\phi)\leq t}\mu_{f}(\phi)=\sup_{\phi:\int\phi{\rm d}\mu\leq t}\int\phi f{\rm d}\mu,
(4)
where the suprema in (4) are over all measurable
\phi:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, this
concentration spectrum completely characterizes the optimal tradeoff
between two types of errors in the hypothesis testing between two
probability measures \mu_{f} and \mu. It is known that (see,
e.g., [35])
\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{f}(t)
\displaystyle={\rm conc\,}\mathfrak{D}_{f}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}f_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v,
(5)
where {\rm conc\,}g denotes the upper concave envelope of a function
g.
Another related quantity is called the E_{\gamma}-divergence [29].
For two probability measures P,Q,
\displaystyle E_{\gamma}(P\|Q)
\displaystyle:=\max_{A}\{P(A)-\gamma Q(A)\}
\displaystyle=P\{{\rm d}P/{\rm d}Q>\gamma\}-\gamma Q\{{\rm d}P/{\rm d}Q>\gamma\}
\displaystyle=\int[{\rm d}P/{\rm d}Q-\gamma]^{+}\mathrm{d}Q,
where [x]^{+}:=\max\{0,x\}.
Proposition 2.2.
[23, Proposition H.1.a]
Let f and g be nonnegative integrable functions on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu).
Then, the following conditions are equivalent.
1.
f\prec g;
2.
\mathfrak{C}_{f}(t)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{g}(t),\;\forall t\geq 0;
3.
\int\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\int\Phi(g)\mathrm{d}\mu for all continuous
convex functions \Phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R} for which the
integrals exist;
4.
\int_{t}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{f}(s){\rm d}s\leq\int_{t}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{g}(s){\rm d}s,\;\forall t\geq 0;
5.
E_{\gamma}(\mu_{f}\|\mu)\leq E_{\gamma}(\mu_{g}\|\mu), i.e., \int[f-\gamma]^{+}\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\int[g-\gamma]^{+}\mathrm{d}\mu,\;\forall\gamma\geq 0.
The concept of majorization can be extended to a pair of functions
defined on two totally different measure spaces.
Definition 2.3.
Let f and g be nonnegative integrable
functions respectively defined on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu)
and (\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},\nu). The function f is
majorized by g, denoted f\prec g, if
1.
\int_{0}^{t}f_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v\leq\int_{0}^{t}g_{\downarrow}(v){\rm d}v,\;\forall t\geq 0,
where f_{\downarrow} is defined in (2) with respect to
\mu and g_{\downarrow} is defined similarly but with respect
to \nu;
2.
\int_{\mathcal{X}}f{\rm d}\mu=\int_{\mathcal{Y}}g{\rm d}\nu.
Although in this general definition, f and g are defined on
two different measure spaces, their decreasing rearrangements f_{\downarrow}
and g_{\downarrow} are defined on the same one, i.e., (\mathbb{R}_{+},\Sigma_{\mathbb{R}_{+}},\lambda). Clearly, the decreasing
rearrangements of f_{\downarrow} and g_{\downarrow} with respect
to the Lebesgue measure \lambda are f_{\downarrow} and g_{\downarrow}
themselves. Hence, according to Definition 2.3, we
arrive at the following observation.
Proposition 2.4.
Let f and g be nonnegative integrable
functions respectively defined on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu)
and (\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},\nu). Then, f\prec g if
and only if f_{\downarrow}\prec g_{\downarrow}.
In this paper, we focus on the integral \int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu
for a given measurable function \Phi. The following well known result shows
that this integral can be expressed as the integral of \Phi(f_{\downarrow}).
Proposition 2.5.
Let f be a nonnegative measurable function
defined on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu).
such that its distribution function is finite on (0,\infty). Then,
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\Phi(f_{\downarrow})\mathrm{d}\lambda,
(6)
for any measurable (not necessarily convex) function \Phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R},
for which at least one of (equivalently, both of) the integrals exists.
By definition, the distribution function of f w.r.t. \mu is identical to the distribution function of f_{\downarrow} w.r.t. \lambda. Moreover, a distribution function that takes finite values on (0,\infty) determines a unique Borel measure on (0,\infty) (see e.g., [14, Theorem 1.16]), and the measure of \{0\} is also determined by the distribution function. So, the measures \mu\circ f^{-1} and \lambda\circ f_{\downarrow}^{-1} are identical.
On the other hand, for any measurable function \Phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R},
\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu
\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\Phi\mathrm{d}(\mu\circ f^{-1})=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\Phi\mathrm{d}(\lambda\circ f_{\downarrow}^{-1})=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{+}}\Phi(f_{\downarrow})\mathrm{d}\lambda.
∎By Propositions 2.2, 2.4,
and 2.5, in order to compare two integrals \int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu
and \int_{\mathcal{Y}}\Phi(g)\mathrm{d}\nu for a continuous convex
function \Phi, it suffices to restrict our attention to the majorization
relation between f_{\downarrow} and g_{\downarrow}.
Proposition 2.6.
Let f and g be nonnegative integrable
functions respectively defined on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu)
and (\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},\nu). Then, the following
conditions are equivalent.
1.
f\prec g;
2.
f_{\downarrow}\prec g_{\downarrow};
3.
\mathfrak{C}_{f}(t)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{g}(t),\;\forall t\geq 0;
4.
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\Phi(g)\mathrm{d}\nu
for all continuous convex functions \Phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R}
for which the integrals exist;
5.
\int_{t}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{f}(s){\rm d}s\leq\int_{t}^{\infty}\mathfrak{m}_{g}(s){\rm d}s,\;\forall t\geq 0;
6.
E_{\gamma}(\mu_{f}\|\mu)\leq E_{\gamma}(\nu_{g}\|\nu), i.e., \int_{\mathcal{X}}[f-\gamma]^{+}\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\int_{\mathcal{Y}}[g-\gamma]^{+}\mathrm{d}\nu,\;\forall\gamma\geq 0.
The concept of majorization can be extended to the relation between
a set of functions and a function.
Definition 2.7.
Let \mathcal{F} be a set of nonnegative functions on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu)
and g be a nonnegative function on (\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},\nu).
We say \mathcal{F} is majorized by g (and write \mathcal{F}\prec g)
if f\prec g for all f\in\mathcal{F}.
Proposition 2.8.
Let \mathcal{F} be a set of nonnegative
functions on (\mathcal{X},\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}},\mu) and g be
a nonnegative function on (\mathcal{Y},\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}},\nu)
such that \mathcal{F}\prec g. Then, for any continuous convex function
\Phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\to\mathbb{R},
\int_{\mathcal{X}}\Phi(f)\mathrm{d}\mu\leq\int_{\mathcal{Y}}\Phi(g)\mathrm{d}\nu,\;\forall f\in\mathcal{F}.
3 Majorization for Noise Operators
We now focus on the hypercube \{0,1\}^{n} and investigate the majorization for T_{\rho}f with Boolean functions f. Let \mu be
the uniform distribution on \{0,1\}^{n}. We say f is a Boolean
function if it is a function f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} for some n.
Denote \mu(f):=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[f].
Definition 3.1.
Given \alpha,\rho\in[0,1], we denote \mathcal{F}_{\alpha,\rho} (or
briefly, \mathcal{F}_{\alpha}) as the set of T_{\rho}f for
Boolean functions f with mean \mu(f)=\alpha.
The concentration spectrum of T_{\rho}f is
\displaystyle\mathfrak{D}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)
\displaystyle=\max_{\textrm{Bool }\phi:\,\mu(\phi)\leq\beta}\int\phi T_{\rho}f{\rm d}\mu,
(7)
and its smooth version is
\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)
\displaystyle=\max_{\phi:\mu(\phi)\leq\beta}\int\phi T_{\rho}f{\rm d}\mu,
(8)
where the maximization in (8) is over all
\phi:\{0,1\}^{n}\to[0,1] such that \mu(\phi)\leq\beta. By the fundamental theorem of linear programming, these two functions coincide when \beta\in 2^{-n}[2^{n}].
A concept related to these two quantities is
the maximal noise stability.
For \alpha,\beta\in 2^{-n}[2^{n}],
define the maximal
noise stability at (\alpha,\beta) as
\mathbf{S}_{n}(\alpha,\beta):=\max_{\textrm{Bool }f,\phi:\,\mu(f)=\alpha,\mu(\phi)=\beta}\int\phi T_{\rho}f{\rm d}\mu,
where the subscript n refers to the dimension.
In the following, we show that \mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)\leq\lim_{m\to\infty}\mathbf{S}_{m}(\alpha,\beta_{m}) holds for any \beta\in[0,1] and any sequence \beta_{m} such that \beta_{m}\in 2^{-m}[2^{m}] and \beta_{m}\to\beta,
where \alpha is the mean of f.
Combining this inequality with Proposition 2.6 implies the following relation between noise stability and majorization for the noise operator.
Proposition 3.2 (Relation Between Majorization and Noise Stability).
Let \Theta be an upper bound on \mathbf{S}_{n},\forall n\geq 1, which satisfies that given \alpha, \Theta(\alpha,\beta) is absolutely continuous
and nondecreasing in \beta, and \Theta(\alpha,0)=0. Then, for
any \rho,\alpha\in[0,1], it holds that \mathcal{F}_{\alpha}\prec\theta_{\alpha},
where for \beta\in[0,1],
\theta_{\alpha}(\beta):=\frac{\partial\Theta(\alpha,\beta)}{\partial\beta}.
(9)
Remark 3.3.
Although this proposition is stated for the Bonami-Beckner operator
on the hypercube, it in fact can be straightforwardly generalized
to an arbitrary semigroup operator on an arbitrary space.
Since \beta\in[0,1]\mapsto\Theta(\alpha,\beta) is nondecreasing, it is differentiable almost everywhere. By the fundamental theorem of Lebesgue integral calculus, \Theta(\alpha,\beta)=\int_{0}^{\beta}\frac{\partial\Theta(\alpha,t)}{\partial t}{\rm d}t.
Let m\geq n. A Boolean function f on the (discrete) n-cube can be viewed as a Boolean function
on the m-cube which only depends on the first n coordinates.
This yields that
T_{\rho}f (with T_{\rho}=T_{\rho}^{(n)}), if viewed as the function T_{\rho}^{(m)}f on the m-cube, also only depends on the first n coordinates. From this view, we can rewrite
\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)
\displaystyle=\max_{\phi:\mu^{(m)}(\phi)\leq\beta}\int\phi T_{\rho}f{\rm d}\mu^{(m)},
(10)
where the maximization in (10) is over all
\phi:\{0,1\}^{m}\to[0,1] such that \mu^{(m)}(\phi)\leq\beta.
This formula follows since, on one hand, if we view a feasible solution \phi to the maximization in (8) as the corresponding function on \{0,1\}^{m} that only depends on the first n coordinates, then \phi is also feasible to the maximization in (10), which implies that the LHS in (10) is smaller than or equal to the RHS; on the other hand, for a feasible solution \phi to
the maximization in (10), if we convert it to the function (x_{1},...,x_{n})\mapsto\mathbb{E}[\phi(x_{1},...,x_{n},X_{n+1},...,X_{m})] on the n-cube, then the resulting function is feasible to the maximization in (8) and also admits the same objective value as the one in (10), which implies that the LHS in (10) is larger than or equal to the RHS.
Obviously, the optimization in (10) is a linear program (viewing \phi as a vector (\phi(\mathbf{x}):\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{m})), and by the fundamental theorem of linear programming, the optimal value is attained at some vertex (or extreme point) of the feasible region. For \beta\in 2^{-m}[2^{m}], a vertex (i.e., an extreme point) of the feasible region must satisfy that \phi(\mathbf{x})=0 or 1 for all \mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^{m}, which corresponds to a Boolean function on \{0,1\}^{m}.
That is, for such \beta, \mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta) is attained by a Boolean function \phi with mean \beta, and hence,
\mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)\leq\mathbf{S}_{m}(\alpha,\beta), where \alpha is the mean of f. By assumption,
for such \beta,
\mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)\leq\Theta(\alpha,\beta).
Since \bigcup_{m\geq n}2^{-m}[2^{m}] is dense in [0,1] and
both these two functions are continuous in \beta, this inequality can be extended to all
\beta\in[0,1].
Furthermore, by the definition of smooth concentration spectrum, \mathfrak{C}_{\theta_{\alpha}}(\beta)\geq\int_{0}^{\beta}\frac{\partial\Theta(\alpha,t)}{\partial t}{\rm d}t=\Theta(\alpha,\beta).
Combining the two inequalities above yields \mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f}(\beta)\leq\mathfrak{C}_{\theta_{\alpha}}(\beta)
for all \beta\in[0,1]. Combined with Proposition 2.6,
these imply \mathcal{F}_{\alpha}\prec\theta_{\alpha}.
∎
A well-known upper bound on the maximal noise stability is given by
the small-set expansion theorem [26, p.280],
which states that
\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{n}(\alpha,\beta)
\displaystyle\leq\Theta_{0}(\alpha,\beta):=\begin{cases}\exp\left(-\frac{s^{2}+t^{2}-2\rho st}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\right),&\rho s\leq t\leq s/\rho,\\
\exp(-\frac{s^{2}}{2}),&0\leq t\leq\rho s,\\
\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}),&t\geq s/\rho,\end{cases}
(11)
where \alpha=\exp(-\frac{s^{2}}{2}) and \beta=\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2})
with s,t\geq 0.
Combining (11) with the fact that
\int\phi T_{\rho}f{\rm d}\mu=\mu(\phi)+\mu(f)-1+\int(1-\phi)T_{\rho}(1-f){\rm d}\mu,
we obtain that
\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{n}(\alpha,\beta)\leq\Theta(\alpha,\beta)
\displaystyle:=\min\{\Theta_{0}(\alpha,\beta),\alpha+\beta-1+\Theta_{0}(1-\alpha,1-\beta)\}.
The upper bound \Theta is simplified in the following proposition.
Denote s=\sqrt{-2\ln\alpha}, t=\sqrt{-2\ln\beta},
\hat{s}=\sqrt{-2\ln(1-\alpha)}, and \hat{t}=\sqrt{-2\ln(1-\beta)}, i.e., \alpha=\exp(-\frac{s^{2}}{2})=1-\exp(-\frac{\hat{s}^{2}}{2})
and \beta=\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2})=1-\exp(-\frac{\hat{t}^{2}}{2}).
Denote
\displaystyle A_{0}
\displaystyle=\{0\leq t\leq\rho s\},A_{1}=\{\rho s\leq t\leq s/\rho\},A_{2}=\{t\geq s/\rho\},
\displaystyle B_{0}
\displaystyle=\{0\leq\hat{t}\leq\rho\hat{s}\},B_{1}=\{\rho\hat{s}\leq\hat{t}\leq\hat{s}/\rho\},B_{2}=\{\hat{t}\geq\hat{s}/\rho\}.
Proposition 3.4.
For \alpha,\beta\in[0,1], it holds that
\Theta_{0}(\alpha,\beta)\leq\alpha+\beta-1+\Theta_{0}(1-\alpha,1-\beta)
if \alpha+\beta\leq 1; the inequality is reversed if \alpha+\beta>1. As a consequence,
\displaystyle\Theta(\alpha,\beta)
\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\Theta_{0}(\alpha,\beta),&\alpha+\beta\leq 1\\
\alpha+\beta-1+\Theta_{0}(1-\alpha,1-\beta),&\alpha+\beta>1\end{cases}
(12)
\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2}),&A_{2}\cap B_{0},\\
\exp\left(-\frac{s^{2}+t^{2}-2\rho st}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\right),&A_{1}\cap\{\alpha+\beta\leq 1\},\\
\exp(-\frac{s^{2}}{2})+\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2})-1+\exp\left(-\frac{\hat{s}^{2}+\hat{t}^{2}-2\rho\hat{s}\hat{t}}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\right),&B_{1}\cap\{\alpha+\beta>1\},\\
\exp(-\frac{s^{2}}{2}),&A_{0}\cap B_{2}.\end{cases}
(13)
The proof of this proposition is given in Appendix A.
These regions A_{i},B_{i},i=0,1,2 and the function \Theta are plotted in Fig. 2.
Here \alpha+\beta\leq 1 is equivalent to t\geq\hat{s} (or s\geq\hat{t}). Moreover, \Theta is continuous and piecewise continuously differentiable, and hence it is absolutely continuous.
Fig 2: Illustration of the regions A_{i},B_{i},i=0,1,2 in the left subfigure and the function \Theta given in
(13) in the right subfigure.
Combining Proposition 3.2 and the explicit bound on noise stability given in (13) yields an explicit function that majorizes the noise operator.
Proposition 3.5 (Majorization for Noise Operator).
For any \rho,\alpha\in[0,1], it holds that \mathcal{F}_{\alpha}\prec\theta_{\alpha},
where for \beta\in[0,1],
\displaystyle\theta_{\alpha}(\beta)
\displaystyle:=\frac{\partial\Theta(\alpha,\beta)}{\partial\beta}=\begin{cases}1,&A_{2}\cap B_{0},\\
\displaystyle\frac{t-\rho s}{(1-\rho^{2})t}\exp\left(-\frac{(s-\rho t)^{2}}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\right),&A_{1}\cap\{\alpha+\beta\leq 1\},\\
\displaystyle 1-\frac{\hat{t}-\rho\hat{s}}{(1-\rho^{2})\hat{t}}\exp\left(-\frac{(\hat{s}-\rho\hat{t})^{2}}{2(1-\rho^{2})}\right),&B_{1}\cap\{\alpha+\beta>1\},\\
0,&A_{0}\cap B_{2}.\end{cases}
(14)
with \alpha=\exp(-\frac{s^{2}}{2})=1-\exp(-\frac{\hat{s}^{2}}{2})
and \beta=\exp(-\frac{t^{2}}{2})=1-\exp(-\frac{\hat{t}^{2}}{2}).
We have investigated the majorization of T_{\rho}f for Boolean functions f in the above. We next generalize it to the case with f replaced by a mixture of Boolean functions.
For Boolean functions f_{i},i\in[k] and a vector \vec{\lambda}:=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},...,\lambda_{k})
with nonnegative real numbers \lambda_{i}, define f_{\vec{\lambda}}:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}f_{i}.
We now investigate the majorization for T_{\rho}f_{\vec{\lambda}}.
Definition 3.6.
Given \rho,\vec{\lambda}:=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},...,\lambda_{k}),\vec{\alpha}:=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...,\alpha_{k}),
we denote \mathcal{F}_{\vec{\lambda},\vec{\alpha}} as the set of
T_{\rho}f_{\vec{\lambda}} for Boolean functions f_{i},i\in[k]
with mean \mu(f_{i})=\alpha_{i},\forall i\in[k].
Following the proofs of Propositions 3.2 and 3.5 (specifically, showing that \mathfrak{C}_{T_{\rho}f_{\vec{\lambda}}}(\beta)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{S}_{n}(\alpha_{i},\beta)\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\Theta(\alpha_{i},\beta)), we obtain the following proposition.
Proposition 3.7.
Given any \rho\in[0,1],\vec{\lambda}\in[0,1]^{k},\vec{\alpha}\in[0,1]^{k},
it holds that \mathcal{F}_{\vec{\lambda},\vec{\alpha}}\prec\theta_{\vec{\lambda},\vec{\alpha}},
where
\theta_{\vec{\lambda},\vec{\alpha}}(\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\theta_{\alpha_{i}}(\beta)
with \theta_{\alpha} given in (14).
As a consequence of this proposition, a bound on the \Phi-stability for the mixture function f_{\vec{\lambda}} can be obtained.
Corollary 3.8 (Bound on \Phi-Stability).
Let \Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous
convex function. For any Boolean functions f_{i},i\in[k] with
mean \mu(f_{i})=\alpha_{i}, it holds that
\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\Phi(T_{\rho}f_{\vec{\lambda}})]\leq\int_{0}^{1}\Phi(\theta_{\vec{\lambda},\vec{\alpha}}(\beta)){\rm d}\beta.
4 Local Optimality of Dictatorships
4.1 \Phi-Stability
We next apply the majorization results derived above to investigate the local optimality
of dictator functions in the noise stability problem.
For ease of presentation, we rewrite the hypercube as \{\pm 1\}^{n}, where 0,1 in the original hypercube \{0,1\}^{n} are respectively mapped to 1,-1.
We use \mathbf{x}=x_{[n]}=(x_{1},...,x_{n})
to denote a length-n vector. We denote the Bonami-Beckner operator
by T_{\rho}=T_{\rho}^{(n)}, and the uniform measure on \{\pm 1\}^{n}
by \mu=\mu^{(n)}. For a Boolean function f, denote A=f^{-1}(1),
i.e., the support of f. Denote the subcubes C_{i}:=\{\mathbf{x}:x_{i}=1\},i\in[n].
The distance between A and C_{i} is
d_{i}(f):=\mu(A\Delta C_{i}),
where \Delta is the symmetric difference. It is easy to verify
that
d_{i}(f)=\|f-1_{C_{i}}\|_{1},
where \|\phi\|_{1}:=\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[|\phi|] is the L_{1}-norm. Hence, d_{i}(f)
represents the distance between f and the dictator function 1_{C_{i}}.
Denote the Fourier coefficients of f as
\hat{f}_{S}:=\mathbb{E}[f(\mathbf{X})\chi_{S}(\mathbf{X})],S\subseteq[n]
where \chi_{S}(\mathbf{X})=\Pi_{i\in S}X_{i},S\subseteq[n] form an orthogonal Fourier basis (on \{-1,1\}^{n}).
Then, in terms of Fourier analysis, d_{i}(f) can be also expressed as
d_{i}(f)=\frac{1}{2}-\hat{f}_{\{i\}}.
Denote
\tilde{d}_{i}(f):=\min\{d_{i}(f),1-d_{i}(f)\},
which represents the distance in the L_{1} sense between f and the set of dictator functions \{1_{C_{i}},1_{C_{i}^{c}}\}. Similarly, the quantity
\tilde{d}(f):=\min_{i\in[n]}\tilde{d}_{i}(f)
(15)
is the (minimum) distance between the balanced Boolean function f and the set of dictator functions.
We are ready to state our first main result, which provides a bound on the \Phi-stability in terms of the distance \tilde{d}_{i}(f) or \tilde{d}(f).
Theorem 4.1 (Bound on \Phi-Stability).
Let \Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} be a continuous
convex function. For any balanced Boolean function f, it holds
that
\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\Phi(T_{\rho}f)]\leq\min_{i\in[n]}\Gamma(\tilde{d}_{i}(f))\leq\Gamma(\tilde{d}(f)),
(16)
where for \epsilon\in[0,1],
\Gamma(\epsilon):=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\left(\Phi(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\theta_{1-\epsilon}(\beta)+\frac{1-\rho}{2}\theta_{\epsilon}(\beta))+\Phi(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\theta_{1-\epsilon}(\beta)+\frac{1+\rho}{2}\theta_{\epsilon}(\beta))\right){\rm d}\beta,
with \theta_{\epsilon} and \theta_{1-\epsilon} given in (9).
Firstly, note that for any i\in[n], any balanced Boolean function
f can be written as
f(\mathbf{x})=1\{x_{i}=1\}f_{+}(x_{\backslash i})+1\{x_{i}=-1\}f_{-}(x_{\backslash i}),
(17)
where x_{\backslash i}:=(x_{1},...,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},...,x_{n})\in\{\pm 1\}^{n-1},
and f_{+}(x_{\backslash i}):=f(x_{i\mapsto 1}), f_{-}(x_{\backslash i}):=f(x_{i\mapsto-1}) with x_{i\mapsto a}=(x_{1},...,x_{i-1},a,x_{i+1},...,x_{n}),a\in\{\pm 1\} are Boolean functions defined on \{\pm 1\}^{n-1}.
So, \mu^{(n-1)}(f_{+})=1-d_{i}(f), \mu^{(n-1)}(f_{-})=d_{i}(f), and we can write
T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})=\begin{cases}T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{+}(x_{\backslash i}),&x_{i}=1\\
T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{-}(x_{\backslash i}),&x_{i}=-1\end{cases},
(18)
where
g_{+}:=\frac{1+\rho}{2}f_{+}+\frac{1-\rho}{2}f_{-},\quad g_{-}:=\frac{1-\rho}{2}f_{+}+\frac{1+\rho}{2}f_{-}.
The \Phi-stability of f is then
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\Phi(T_{\rho}f)]
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\Phi(T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{+}(X_{\backslash i}))+\Phi(T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{-}(X_{\backslash i}))\Bigr].
(19)
By Corollary 3.8, we obtain
\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[\Phi(T_{\rho}f)]\leq\min_{i\in[n]}\Gamma(d_{i}(f)).
(20)
Since \Gamma(\epsilon)=\Gamma(1-\epsilon), (20)
implies (16).
∎
When we take \epsilon\downarrow 0, Theorem 4.1
implies the following asymptotic bound. The proof is provided in Appendix
B.
Theorem 4.2 (Asymptotic Bound).
Let \Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} be continuous
convex on [0,1] and twice continuously differentiable on (0,1).
Let \rho\in(0,1). Then, for any c\in(\rho,1/\rho) it holds
that as \epsilon\downarrow 0,
\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]\leq A_{0}-A_{1}\epsilon+A_{2}(1+o(1))\epsilon^{\frac{2}{1+\rho^{2}}}\sqrt{2\ln\frac{1}{\epsilon}}+O(\epsilon^{c^{2}}),
for any balanced Boolean function f such that \tilde{d}_{i}(f)=\epsilon
for some i\in[n], where
\displaystyle A_{0}
\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\Phi(\frac{1+\rho}{2})+\Phi(\frac{1-\rho}{2})\right),
\displaystyle A_{1}
\displaystyle=\frac{\rho}{2}\left(\Phi^{\prime}(\frac{1+\rho}{2})-\Phi^{\prime}(\frac{1-\rho}{2})\right),
\displaystyle A_{2}
\displaystyle=\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{\rho}{4}\sqrt{\frac{1-\rho^{2}}{1+\rho^{2}}}\left(\Phi^{\prime\prime}(\frac{1+\rho}{2})+\Phi^{\prime\prime}(\frac{1-\rho}{2})\right).
Remark 4.3.
If \Phi^{\prime\prime} is continuous and hence bounded on [0,1], the bound above can be sharpened into that
\displaystyle\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]
\displaystyle=A_{0}-A_{1}\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{\frac{2}{1+\rho^{2}}})
for any balanced Boolean function f. This can be seen as follows.
Any balanced Boolean function f can be expressed as f(\mathbf{x})=1\{x_{i}=1\}+g(\mathbf{x}),
where g(\mathbf{x})=1\{x_{i}=-1\}1_{B_{2}}(x_{\backslash i})-1\{x_{i}=1\}1_{B_{1}}(x_{\backslash i})
for some sets B_{1},B_{2}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{n-1} with same probability
\epsilon. Given f, by Taylor’s theorem,
\displaystyle\Phi(T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x}))
\displaystyle=\Phi(\frac{1+\rho x_{i}}{2})+\Phi^{\prime}(\frac{1+\rho x_{i}}{2})T_{\rho}g(\mathbf{x})+\frac{1}{2}\Phi^{\prime\prime}(\xi)(T_{\rho}g(\mathbf{x}))^{2},
where \xi depends on \mathbf{x}. If \Phi^{\prime\prime} is bounded, then
taking expectation for two sides of the equation above yields that
\displaystyle\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]
\displaystyle=A_{0}-A_{1}\epsilon+O(\mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}g)^{2}]),
where by the hypercontractivity inequality (stated in the following lemma), \mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}g)^{2}]\leq\|g\|_{1+\rho^{2}}^{2}=(2\epsilon)^{\frac{2}{1+\rho^{2}}}.
So, for this case,
\displaystyle\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]
\displaystyle=A_{0}-A_{1}\epsilon+O(\epsilon^{\frac{2}{1+\rho^{2}}}).
Although this asymptotic equality is sharper, it requires the boundness
of \Phi^{\prime\prime}. Unfortunately, the most interesting cases, \Phi_{q}
and \Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}} with q<2, do not satisfy this condition.
The hypercontractivity inequality mentioned above is given below.
Lemma 4.4 (Hypercontractivity Inequality; see e.g., [26]).
Let T_{\rho} be the noise operator defined on \{\pm 1\}^{n}. Then,
for q>1, it holds that
\|T_{\rho}g\|_{q}\leq\|g\|_{p} for all function g:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}
where p=1+(q-1)\rho^{2}.
Note that A_{0} in Theorem 4.2 is exactly the \Phi-stability of dictator functions.
Moreover, if \Phi is strictly convex, then A_{1}>0. So, Theorem
4.2 implies the local optimality of dictator functions.
Theorem 4.5 (Local Optimality of Dictator Functions).
Let \Phi:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R} be a twice continuously
differentiable and strictly convex function. Let \rho\in(0,1).
Then, there exists \epsilon>0 such that for any balanced Boolean
function f satisfying 0<\min_{i\in[n]}\tilde{d}_{i}(f)\leq\epsilon,
it holds that
\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]<\mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f_{\mathrm{d}}].
In other words, dictator functions are locally optimal in maximizing
the \Phi-stability.
4.2 q-Stability
Theorem 4.5 shows that for sufficiently small
\epsilon>0, dictator functions have larger \Phi-stability than
any balanced Boolean function f satisfying 0<\min_{i\in[n]}\tilde{d}_{i}(f)\leq\epsilon.
The value of \epsilon here can be determined by checking our
proof, but the final expression seems very complicated. However,
if we focus on the q-stability, then we can obtain an explicit
expression for such an \epsilon by using hypercontractivity
inequalities. Before stating this result, we need introduce some notations.
For \epsilon\in[0,1], define
\Gamma_{q}(\epsilon):=\frac{\gamma_{q}(\epsilon)-\frac{1}{2}}{q-1},
for q>0 but q\neq 1, where
\gamma_{q}(\epsilon):=\frac{1}{2}\left(\epsilon+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2\epsilon)\right)^{q/p}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\epsilon+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2\epsilon)\right)^{q/p}
with p=1+(q-1)\rho^{2}. For q=1, define
\displaystyle\Gamma_{1}(\epsilon)
\displaystyle:=\lim_{q\to 1}\Gamma_{q}(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{2}(1-\rho^{2})h\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}+\rho\epsilon\right)+(\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon)\rho^{2}h\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right),
where recall that h(t)=t\ln t+(1-t)\ln(1-t).
Theorem 4.6 (Bound on q-Stability).
Let f be a balanced Boolean function.
Then, for any q>0 and i\in[n], it holds that
\mathbf{Stab}_{q}[f]\leq\Gamma_{q}(\tilde{d}_{i}(f)).
(21)
Remark 4.7.
This theorem immediately implies a similar result for the symmetric
q-stability, i.e.,
\displaystyle\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]
\displaystyle\leq 2\Gamma_{q}(\tilde{d}_{i}(f)),\;q>0.
We first consider the case q>1. Using (19) with \Phi set to t\mapsto t^{q}, we can write
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[(T_{\rho}f)^{q}]=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[(T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{+})^{q}]+\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[(T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{-})^{q}]\right).
(22)
To upper bound the RHS above, we need the hypercontractivity inequality, restated in Lemma 4.4. That is,
\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[(T_{\rho}g)^{q}]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[g^{p}]^{q/p},\;\forall g,
where p=1+(q-1)\rho^{2}.
By this inequality,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[(T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{+})^{q}]
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{+}^{p}]^{q/p},
(23)
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[(T_{\rho}^{(n-1)}g_{-})^{q}]
\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{-}^{p}]^{q/p}.
(24)
We now upper bound \mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{+}^{p}] and \mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{-}^{p}].
Let A_{+}=\operatorname{supp}(f_{+}) and A_{-}=\operatorname{supp}(f_{-}). So, \mu^{(n-1)}(A_{+})=1-d_{i}(f),
\mu^{(n-1)}(A_{-})=d_{i}(f). Then,
\displaystyle g_{+}
\displaystyle=1_{A_{+}\cap A_{-}}+\frac{1+\rho}{2}1_{A_{+}\backslash A_{-}}+\frac{1-\rho}{2}1_{A_{-}\backslash A_{+}},
\displaystyle g_{-}
\displaystyle=1_{A_{+}\cap A_{-}}+\frac{1-\rho}{2}1_{A_{+}\backslash A_{-}}+\frac{1+\rho}{2}1_{A_{-}\backslash A_{+}}.
So,
\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{+}^{p}]=\mu^{(n-1)}(A_{+}\cap A_{-})+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}\mu^{(n-1)}(A_{+}\backslash A_{-})+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}\mu^{(n-1)}(A_{-}\backslash A_{+}).
Denote \kappa=\mu^{(n-1)}(A_{+}\cap A_{-})\in[0,\tilde{d}_{i}(f)].
Then,
\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{+}^{p}]=\kappa+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-d_{i}(f)-\kappa)+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(d_{i}(f)-\kappa).
Note that \left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}<1
for p>1. Hence, the RHS is maximized at \kappa=\tilde{d}_{i}(f),
i.e.,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{+}^{p}]
\displaystyle\leq\tilde{d}_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-d_{i}(f)-\tilde{d}_{i}(f))+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(d_{i}(f)-\tilde{d}_{i}(f))
\displaystyle=\begin{cases}d_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2d_{i}(f)),&d_{i}(f)\leq 1/2\\
1-d_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(2d_{i}(f)-1),&d_{i}(f)>1/2\end{cases}.
Similarly,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{-}^{p}]
\displaystyle\leq\begin{cases}d_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2d_{i}(f)),&d_{i}(f)\leq 1/2\\
1-d_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(2d_{i}(f)-1),&d_{i}(f)>1/2\end{cases}.
Combining these estimates with (22) and (24) yields that
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mu}[(T_{\rho}f)^{q}]
\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{+}^{p}]^{q/p}+\mathbb{E}_{\mu^{(n-1)}}[g_{-}^{p}]^{q/p}\right)
\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\left(\tilde{d}_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2\tilde{d}_{i}(f))\right)^{q/p}
\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{1}{2}\left(\tilde{d}_{i}(f)+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2\tilde{d}_{i}(f))\right)^{q/p}.
The inequality in (21) for 0<q<1 follows similarly, but
the reverse hypercontractivity inequality will be applied. Taking the
limit q\downarrow 1 in (21), we obtain the bound on
1-stability.
∎
Based on the bound given in Theorem 4.6, we next provide an explicit range of \tilde{d}(f) for which dictator functions are optimal in maximizing q-stability. Here, recall that \tilde{d}(f) is the minimum distance in the L_{1} sense between the balanced Boolean function f and the set of dictator functions.
That is, given q>0, our interest lies in determining the values of \epsilon for which the inequality
\displaystyle\Gamma_{q}(\epsilon)
\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
(25)
holds.
Theorem 4.6 implies the optimality of dictator functions over all balanced Boolean functions with \epsilon=\tilde{d}(f) satisfying (25). This recovers and strengthens Theorem 4.5.
To this end, we introduce the following notations. For q\in(0,\infty)\backslash\{1\}
and \rho\in(0,1), let \epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho) be the unique value
\epsilon in (0,1/2] attaining the equality in (25)
if such \epsilon exists, i.e., the unique solution
in (0,1/2] (if the solution exists) to the equation
\left(\epsilon+\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2\epsilon)\right)^{q/p}+\left(\epsilon+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{p}(1-2\epsilon)\right)^{q/p}=\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{q}+\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{q}
(26)
with p=1+(q-1)\rho^{2}. By continuous extension, let \epsilon_{q}^{*}(0):=\lim_{\rho\downarrow 0}\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)=1-\ln 2,
and let \epsilon_{q}^{*}(1):=\lim_{\rho\uparrow 1}\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)
which is the unique solution in (0,1/2] to the equation
2(q-1)h(\epsilon)=\epsilon q^{2}
(if the solution exists). Note that the base of the logarithm in the definition
of h is e.
By continuous extension, for q=1, let \epsilon^{*}(\rho):=\epsilon_{1}^{*}(\rho)
be the unique solution in (0,1/2] to the equation
h\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}+\rho\epsilon\right)=\left(1+\frac{2\rho^{2}\epsilon}{1-\rho^{2}}\right)h\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right),
(27)
where recall that -h is the binary entropy function.
Since the LHS in (26) and the LHS in (27) are
strictly convex in \epsilon for q\geq 1 and strictly
concave in \epsilon for 0<q<1, there are at most two solutions
to the equation in (26) or the equation in (27).
Obviously, \epsilon=0 is one of them. So, there is at most one
solution other than 0. Moreover, this solution must be \leq 1/2
if it exists. This is because, the LHS in (26) with \epsilon=1/2
is larger than the RHS for q>1, and is smaller than the
RHS for 0<q<1, which follows by substituting dictator functions
into the forward and reverse hypercontractivity inequalities. In fact,
numerical results show that for q\geq 6.5 or q<1, there always
exists \rho\in(0,1) for which no solution in (0,1/2] to the
equation in (26) exists. However, for 1\leq q\leq 6.4,
it seems that there always exists a solution in (0,1/2] to the
equation in (26) or (27) (and hence, it is unique).
For q\in[1,2], we provide a rigorous proof for this point in the
following lemma. The function \epsilon_{1}^{*}(\rho) is plotted
in Fig. 3.
Fig 3: The plot of the function \epsilon_{1}^{*}.
Lemma 4.8.
The following hold.
1.
For q=1 and \rho\in(0,1), there is a unique solution in (0,1/2]
to the equation in (27).
2.
For q\in(1,2] and \rho\in(0,1), there is a unique solution in
(0,1/2] to the equation in (26).
Moreover, for q=1, \epsilon_{1}^{*}(\rho) satisfies monotonicity,
as observed from Fig. 3.
Lemma 4.9.
For q=1, \epsilon_{1}^{*}(\rho) is
decreasing in \rho\in(0,1).
The proofs of Lemmas 4.8 and 4.9
are respectively provided in Appendices C
and D.
As mentioned above, Theorem 4.6 implies the local optimality of
dictator functions, as shown in the following theorem. Different from Theorem 4.5, the following theorem
provides an explicit expression for a threshold \epsilon.
Theorem 4.10 (Local Optimality of Dictator Functions).
Let q>0 and
\rho\in(0,1) such that \epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho) exists and \epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)>0.
Let f be a balanced Boolean function f satisfying 0\leq\tilde{d}(f)\leq\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho), where recall that \tilde{d}(f):=\min_{i\in[n]}\tilde{d}_{i}(f).
Then, it holds that
\displaystyle\mathbf{Stab}_{q}[f]
\displaystyle\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}[f_{\mathrm{d}}].
(28)
In other words, dictator functions maximize the q-stability over all balanced
Boolean functions f such that 0\leq\tilde{d}(f)\leq\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho).
This theorem still holds when the asymmetric q-stability is replaced
by the symmetric q-stability.
5 Global Optimality of Dictatorships
We next investigate the global optimality of dictator functions in
maximizing the q-stability. Specifically, we prove improved bounds
for the Courtade–Kumar conjecture and the Li–Médard conjecture, which
respectively correspond to maximizing the q-stability with q=1
and 1<q<2.
5.1 q-Stability with q=1 (Courtade–Kumar Conjecture)
In this subsection, we focus on the case q=1 and will prove the Courtade–Kumar Conjecture for \rho\in[0,0.914].
Our proof idea is as follows. By Theorem 4.10, dictator functions are locally optimal in maximizing the q-stability. Hence, we only need to consider the Boolean functions far from dictator functions.
Fortunately, due to the spread of the spectrum of such Boolean functions f, the energy of T_{\rho}f
is significantly smaller than the energy of T_{\rho}f_{\mathrm{d}} (especially for small \rho) where f_{\mathrm{d}} is a dictator function. Utilizing this property, the present author established a bound on \Phi-stability in [34], which proves effective for such Boolean functions and hence will serve as a key tool in proving our new bounds.
We first introduce the previous bound derived by the present author in [34].
Define for 0\leq\beta\leq\frac{1}{2},
\omega(\beta):=\min\Big\{\beta^{2}+\varphi(\frac{1}{2}-\beta),\,\frac{\left(1+\sqrt{1+4(\pi-\sqrt{2\pi})\beta}\right)^{2}}{8\pi}\Big\},
(29)
where for 0\leq t\leq 1,
\varphi(t):=\min\{\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}(\tilde{t}),\varphi_{\mathrm{LP}}(\tilde{t})\},
with \tilde{t}:=\min\{t,1-t\} and11
1
Here, the subscript “\mathrm{C}” refers to “Chang”, since
\varphi_{\mathrm{C}} was used to bound the first-level Fourier
weight of a Boolean function in Chang’s lemma [7, 26].
The subscript “\mathrm{LP}” refers to “Linear Programming”,
since \varphi_{\mathrm{LP}} was used to bound the first-level Fourier
weight by linear programming methods [15, 36].
\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathrm{C}}(t)
\displaystyle:=2t^{2}\ln\frac{1}{t},\;0\leq t\leq\frac{1}{2},
\displaystyle\varphi_{\mathrm{LP}}(t)
\displaystyle:=\begin{cases}2t^{2}(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-1),&0<t\leq\frac{1}{4}\\
\frac{t}{2},&\frac{1}{4}\leq t\leq\frac{1}{2}\end{cases}.
The quantity \omega(\beta) in fact forms an upper bound on the first-level Fourier weight of a balanced Boolean function for which a particular first-level Fourier coefficient has absolute value \beta [34]. That is,
\mathbf{W}_{1}:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\hat{f}_{\{i\}}^{2}\leq\omega(\beta)\leq\frac{1}{4}
(30)
holds for all balanced Boolean function f with |\hat{f}_{\{i\}}|=\beta for some i\in[n]. This is a quantitative version of Friedgut-Kalai-Naor (FKN) theorem.
The function \omega is plotted in Fig. 4.
Fig 4: Illustration of the function \omega.
Define for 0\leq\beta\leq\frac{1}{2},
\Upsilon_{\rho}(\beta):=\sup_{(z_{1},z_{2})\in\mathcal{Z}}\gamma(z_{1},z_{2},\beta),
(31)
where
\mathcal{Z}:=\{(z_{1},z_{2}):-\frac{1}{2\rho}<z_{1}\leq z_{2}<\frac{1}{2\rho},0\leq p_{1}\leq\frac{1}{4}+\frac{\beta}{2},0\leq p_{2}\leq\frac{1}{4}-\frac{\beta}{2}\},
(32)
and
\gamma(z_{1},z_{2},\beta):=(1-2p_{1}-2p_{2})\Phi(0)+2p_{1}\Phi(\frac{1}{2}+\rho z_{1})+2p_{2}\Phi(\frac{1}{2}+\rho z_{2}),
with
\displaystyle p_{1}=\frac{(1-\rho)(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega(\beta)+2\beta(1+2\rho z_{2}-\rho^{2}))}{4(1+2\rho z_{1})(1+\rho z_{2}-\rho z_{1}-\rho^{2})},
(33)
\displaystyle p_{2}=\frac{(1-\rho)(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega(\beta)-2\beta(1-2\rho z_{1}-\rho^{2}))}{4(1-2\rho z_{2})(1+\rho z_{2}-\rho z_{1}-\rho^{2})}.
(34)
Theorem 5.1 ([34]).
If \Phi is symmetric
and continuous on [0,1] and differentiable on (0,1) whose derivative
\Phi^{\prime} is increasing and continuous on (0,1), and strictly concave
on (0,\frac{1}{2}], then for any \rho\in(0,1) and any balanced
Boolean function f, it holds that \mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]\leq\Upsilon_{\rho}(\beta),
where \beta=\max_{i\in[n]}|\hat{f}_{\{i\}}|.
This theorem was proven by Boolean Fourier analysis, particularly
by using an energy control technique and a quantitative version of
the Friedgut–Kalai–Naor (FKN) theorem. To be self-contained, here we provide a proof sketch of this theorem. The complete
proof can be found in [34].
Let f be a balanced Boolean function. Recall that \{\hat{f}_{T}:T\subseteq[n]\} are the Fourier coefficients of f.
Denote the degree-k part of f as
f_{k}(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{T\subseteq[n]:|T|=k}\hat{f}_{T}\chi_{T}(\mathbf{x}),
and the degree-k Fourier weight of f as
\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{k}:=\mathbf{W}_{k}[f]
\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}[f_{k}^{2}(\mathbf{X})]=\sum_{T:|T|=k}\hat{f}_{T}^{2},\quad k\in[0:n].
(35)
It is evident that the functions f_{k} for k\in[0:n] are mutually orthogonal, a direct consequence of the orthogonality inherent to the Fourier basis.
Without loss of generality, we assume |\hat{f}_{\{1\}}|\geq|\hat{f}_{\{i\}}|
for all 2\leq i\leq n. If \hat{f}_{\{1\}}\geq 0, denote \beta=\hat{f}_{\{1\}}
and X:=X_{1}; otherwise, \beta:=-\hat{f}_{\{1\}} and X:=-X_{1}.
Hence \beta\geq 0. Define several other random variables:
\displaystyle S
\displaystyle:=f(\mathbf{X})-\frac{1}{2}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}f_{k}(\mathbf{X}),\quad Z:=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\rho^{k-1}f_{k}(\mathbf{X}).
Since \mathbb{E}[SX]=\beta, (S,X) satisfies the following joint distribution
P_{SX}(s,x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1+2\beta}{4},&(s,x)=\pm(1/2,1)\\
\frac{1-2\beta}{4},&(s,x)=\pm(1/2,-1)\end{cases}.
The energy of Z can be controlled as follows:
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]=\mathbf{W}_{1}+\rho^{2}\sum_{k=2}^{n}\rho^{2(k-2)}\mathbf{W}_{k}
\displaystyle\leq(1-\rho)\mathbf{W}_{1}+\rho\left(\mathbf{W}_{1}+\rho\sum_{k=2}^{n}\rho^{k-2}\mathbf{W}_{k}\right)
\displaystyle\leq(1-\rho)\omega(\beta)+\rho\mathbb{E}[SZ],
where in the last line, the quantitative version of FKN theorem in (30) is applied. Moreover, by definition,
\displaystyle\mathbb{E}Z
\displaystyle=0,\quad\mathbb{E}[XZ]=\beta,\quad T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{X})=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\rho^{k}f_{k}(\mathbf{X})=\frac{1}{2}+\rho Z,
Summarizing all the properties listed above on Z, we obtain the following bound on \Phi-stability: \mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]\leq\tilde{\Upsilon}_{\rho}(\beta),
where \tilde{\Upsilon}_{\rho}(\beta) is defined as the supremum of \mathbb{E}[\Phi(\frac{1}{2}+\rho Z)] over all random variables Z (equivalently, over all conditional distributions P_{Z|SX}) defined on any finite set such that
\displaystyle 0\leq\frac{1}{2}+\rho Z\leq 1\textrm{ a.s.},\quad\mathbb{E}Z=0,\quad\mathbb{E}[XZ]=\beta,\quad\mathbb{E}[Z^{2}]\leq(1-\rho)\omega(\beta)+\rho\mathbb{E}[SZ].
(36)
We next simplify the bound \tilde{\Upsilon}_{\rho}(\beta) and prove that \tilde{\Upsilon}_{\rho}(\beta)=\Upsilon_{\rho}(\beta). By a proper version of Carathéodory’s theorem, the optimization in the definition of \tilde{\Upsilon}_{\rho}(\beta) can be converted into a finite-dimensional program and the supremum therein is a maximum, since the feasible region is compact and the objective
and constraint functions are continuous. Moreover, the maximum is attained only
when the last constraint in (36) is an equality.
We can assume that the linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ), a sufficient condition for the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker
(KKT) conditions to be valid, is satisfied by all optimal solutions to this finite program, since all feasible solutions violating the LICQ are suboptimal (more precisely, they cannot be better than the best one satisfying the LICQ). Applying KKT conditions and excluding all suboptimal solutions satisfying these conditions, one can find that the optimal solutions
have the following form:
P_{SXZ}(s,x,z)=\begin{cases}\frac{1+2\beta}{4}-p_{1},&(s,x,z)=\pm(-\frac{1}{2},-1,-\frac{1}{2\rho})\\
p_{1},&(s,x,z)=\pm(-\frac{1}{2},-1,z_{1})\\
\frac{1-2\beta}{4}-p_{2},&(s,x,z)=\pm(\frac{1}{2},-1,\frac{1}{2\rho})\\
p_{2},&(s,x,z)=\pm(\frac{1}{2},-1,z_{2})\end{cases}
for some z_{1},z_{2} such that -\frac{1}{2\rho}\leq z_{1}\leq z_{2}\leq\frac{1}{2\rho}.
For the case of -\frac{1}{2\rho}<z_{1}\leq z_{2}<\frac{1}{2\rho}, solving the last two constraints in (36) (with the last one set to an equality) gives the solution p_{1},p_{2}
in (33) and (34), which yields \Upsilon_{\rho}. The case
z_{1}=-\frac{1}{2\rho} or the case z_{2}=\frac{1}{2\rho} is covered via taking limits.
∎
We in fact use this theorem
to prove that the Courtade–Kumar conjecture (as well as the symmetrized
Li–Médard conjecture) is true for all \rho\in[0,0.46] [34].
The intuition behind the proof given above is that if f is far from dictator
functions, then \beta would be small, due to the following identity |\hat{f}_{\{i\}}|=\frac{1}{2}-\tilde{d}_{i}(f), i.e.,
\beta=\frac{1}{2}-\tilde{d}(f).
By the quantitative version of FKN theorem in (30) and
the energy control (i.e., the last constraint in (36)),
in this case, the energy of Z (defined in the proof sketch above), or equivalently, the energy of T_{\rho}f (i.e., the 2-stability \mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}f)^{2}])
would be small, especially for small \rho. This in
turn decreases the \Phi-stability (due to the facts that \mathbf{Stab}_{\Phi}[f]=\mathbb{E}[\Phi(\frac{1}{2}+\rho Z)] and \Phi is convex). Hence, to maximize the \Phi-stability,
f must be close to or exactly equal to a dictator function.
Bounding the energy of T_{\rho}f is easy for small \rho, but
not easy for large \rho. This is because, when \rho is close to
1, the energy of T_{\rho}f is close to the energy of f (i.e.,
1/2) which is always large. This is the reason why the bound in Theorem 5.1 does not work effectively for small \rho, in the aspect of excluding the Boolean functions close to dictator
functions from being optimal (i.e., showing the local
optimality of dictator functions).
Fortunately, Theorem 4.10 can also serve the same purpose. Specifically, by Theorem 4.10, if
0\leq\tilde{d}(f)\leq\epsilon^{*}(\rho), then
\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}].
On the other hand, if \tilde{d}(f)>\epsilon^{*}(\rho),
i.e.,
\beta=\frac{1}{2}-\tilde{d}(f)<\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon^{*}(\rho),
then by Theorem 5.1 with \Phi=\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}},
\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\max_{\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon^{*}(\rho)]}\Upsilon_{\rho}(\beta).
(37)
So, combining these two cases, we get a bound for the 1-stability:
\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\max\left\{\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}],\max_{\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon^{*}(\rho)]}\Upsilon_{\rho}(\beta)\right\},
(38)
which can be relaxed to the following simple one.
Theorem 5.2.
For
any \rho\in(0,1) and any balanced Boolean function f, it holds
that
\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\max\left\{\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}],\max_{t\in[0,1)}\eta_{1}(t),\max_{t\in[0,1)}\eta_{2}(t)\right\},
(39)
where
\displaystyle\eta_{1}(t)
\displaystyle:=\frac{\left(1-\rho\right)\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega^{*}(\rho)\right)}{2\left(1+t-\rho^{2}\right)}\phi(\frac{1-t}{2}),
\displaystyle\eta_{2}(t)
\displaystyle:=\frac{1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega^{*}(\rho)-(1-2\epsilon^{*}(\rho))\rho^{2}t}{2(1+\rho)(1+t)}\phi(\frac{1-t}{2}),
\displaystyle\omega^{*}(\rho)
\displaystyle:=\max_{\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon^{*}(\rho)]}\omega(\beta),
\displaystyle\phi(s)
\displaystyle:=\frac{\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}(s)}{s}=\frac{s\ln s+(1-s)\ln(1-s)}{s},\,s\in(0,1].
The proof of this theorem is
provided in Appendix E. The last two constraints in (32) have been discarded in proving
the bound in (39), which might make it weaker than the one in (38). However, numerical results indicate that as \rho increases beyond a critical threshold (\rho=0.914...), the value \max\left\{\max_{t\in[0,1)}\eta_{1}(t),\max_{t\in[0,1)}\eta_{2}(t)\right\} surpasses \mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]. Notably, the discarded constraints remain inactive near this critical point. In other words, this simplified bound retains full optimality for the specific purposes of this paper.
Numerical results
also indicate that the bound in (39) is better than the bound in Theorem 5.1 for large \rho, which is intuitively obvious due to the incorporation of Theorem 4.10.
By this theorem, if for a given \rho, the maximum at the RHS of
(39) is no larger than \mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]=\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\frac{1+\rho}{2}),
then dictator functions are globally optimal in maximizing the 1-stability
over all balanced Boolean functions. In [34], we have
already proven that the Courtade–Kumar conjecture is true for \rho\in[0,0.46].
So, here we only focus on the case \rho\geq 0.46.
Corollary 5.3.
If for a given \rho,
\displaystyle 1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega^{*}(\rho)-(1-2\epsilon^{*}(\rho))(2-\rho^{2})
\displaystyle\geq 0,
(40)
\displaystyle\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in[0,1)\end{subarray}}\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega^{*}(\rho)\right)\phi(\frac{1-t}{2})-\left(1+t-\rho^{2}\right)\phi(\frac{1-\rho}{2})\,
\displaystyle\leq 0,
(41)
then \mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
for all balanced Boolean functions f. In particular, if for some
\rho^{*}\in[0.46,1],
\displaystyle\min_{\rho\in[0.46,\rho^{*}]}1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{0}-(1-2\epsilon_{0})(2-\rho^{2})
\displaystyle\geq 0,
(42)
\displaystyle\max_{\rho\in[0.46,\rho^{*}]}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in[0,1)\end{subarray}}\chi(\rho,t)\,
\displaystyle\leq 0,
(43)
where the function \chi is given by
\chi(\rho,t):=\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{0}\right)\phi(\frac{1-t}{2})-\left(1+t-\rho^{2}\right)\phi(\frac{1-\rho}{2}),
\epsilon_{0} is a number such that \epsilon^{*}(\rho)\geq\epsilon_{0},\forall\rho\in[0.46,\rho^{*}], and \omega_{0} is a number such that \omega^{*}(\rho)\leq\omega_{0},\forall\rho\in[0.46,\rho^{*}], then for all \rho\in[0.46,\rho^{*}],
\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
for all balanced Boolean functions f.
Remark 5.4.
Note that t\in[0,1)\mapsto\chi(\rho,t)
is concave (see Lemma E.1), and hence the optimal t attaining the maximum in (43)
is the unique solution t_{\rho}\in(0,1) to the equation
-\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{0}\right)\phi^{\prime}(\frac{1-t}{2})-\phi(\frac{1-\rho}{2})=0.
(44)
It is straightforward to see that \eta_{2}(t)\leq\eta_{1}(t),\forall t\in[0,1) (defined in Theorem 5.2) if (40) holds.
If we can further show \eta_{1}(t)\leq\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\frac{1+\rho}{2}),\forall t\in[0,1),
or equivalently, the condition in (41),
then by Theorem 5.2, \mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
for all balanced Boolean functions f. Since \phi is negative,
the second statement follows obviously.
∎In the following, we analytically verify (42) and numerically verify (43) for proper
choices of \rho^{*} and \omega_{0}. Specifically, we choose
\rho^{*}=0.914,
(45)
for which we observe that \epsilon^{*}(\rho)\geq\epsilon_{0}:=\epsilon^{*}(0.914)=0.195055... and
\omega^{*}(\rho)\leq\omega_{0}:=\omega^{*}(0.914)=\omega(\beta_{0})=0.193026...
for all \rho\in[0.46,0.914], with \beta_{0}=0.175661...
Note that the objective function in (42) is a quadratic polynomial. We hence easily prove that the inequality in (42) holds in this case. On the other hand, using
Matlab, we numerically verify that
\max_{\rho\in[0.46,0.914]}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in[0,1)\end{subarray}}\chi(\rho,t)=-0.00169063...<0,
(46)
with the maximum attained at \rho=0.914 and t=0.663100...
Hence, for all 0.46\leq\rho\leq 0.914, dictator functions maximize
the 1-stability over all balanced Boolean functions. Combining
it with our previous result in [34], we conclude that
for all 0\leq\rho\leq 0.914, dictator functions maximize the 1-stability
over all balanced Boolean functions.
We now use a computer-assisted method to prove the numerical observation
above.
Theorem 5.5.
The optimal value of (46) with \Phi=\Phi_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}
and \rho^{*}=0.914 is negative. In other words, for any \rho\in[0.46,0.914],
it holds that \mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{1}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
for all balanced Boolean functions f.
Combining this theorem with the result in [34] indicates
that dictator functions maximize the 1-stability over all balanced
Boolean functions for all \rho\in[0,0.914].
Theorem 5.6 (Restatement of Theorem 1.5).
The Courtade–Kumar
conjecture is true for all \rho\in[0,0.914].
The Courtade–Kumar conjecture for the case of \rho\in(0.914,1)
is still open.
Our proof idea for Theorem 5.5 is as follows. We first show
that \partial_{\rho}\chi in (46) is bounded on the feasible
region (say, belonging to [-M,M]). Then, for any \rho, \hat{\rho},
and t, it holds that
\chi(\hat{\rho},t)\leq\chi(\rho,t)+M|\hat{\rho}-\rho|.
(47)
That is, if for any \delta>0, we verify \chi(\rho,t)<-\delta
for all \rho\in[0.46,0.914]\cap(\frac{\delta}{M}\mathbb{Z}), then
we can conclude that \chi(\hat{\rho},t)<0 for all \hat{\rho}\in[0.46,0.914].
The detailed proof is provided in Appendix F.
5.2 q-Stability with 1<q<2 (Li–Médard Conjecture)
We next focus on q-stability for 1<q<2 and prove the Li–Médard Conjecture for q\in[1.36,2). We build on the approach used for the case q=1, extending it to the present setting. Specifically, we combine Theorems 4.10 and 5.1 to establish the global optimality of dictator functions. Theorem 4.10 ensures that any extremizer maximizing q-stability among Boolean functions close to some dictator function must itself be a dictator function.
Meanwhile, Theorem 5.1 ensures that any Boolean function sufficiently distant from all dictator functions cannot exhibit a higher q-stability than a dictator function.
We first establish an analogue of Theorem 5.2, i.e., a simplified version of Theorem 5.1, for q-stability. By Theorem
4.10, if 0\leq\tilde{d}(f)\leq\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho),
then \mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}].
On the other hand, if \tilde{d}(f)>\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho),
i.e.,
\beta=\max_{i\in[n]}|\hat{f}_{\{i\}}|=\frac{1}{2}-\tilde{d}(f)<\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho),
then by Theorem 5.1 with \Phi=\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}},
\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\max_{\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)]}\Upsilon_{\rho}(\beta).
(48)
Similarly to the case q=1, we can simplify this bound as follows.
Theorem 5.7.
Let \Phi=\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}. Then, for
any q\in(1,2), \rho\in(0,1), and any balanced Boolean function
f, it holds that
\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\max\left\{\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}],\max_{t\in[0,1]}\eta_{q,1}(t),\max_{t\in[0,1]}\eta_{q,2}(t)\right\},
(49)
where
\displaystyle\eta_{q,1}(t)
\displaystyle:=\frac{\left(1-\rho\right)\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)\right)}{2\left(1+t-\rho^{2}\right)}\phi_{q}(\frac{1-t}{2}),
\displaystyle\eta_{q,2}(t)
\displaystyle:=\frac{1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)-(1-2\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho))\rho^{2}t}{2(1+\rho)(1+t)}\phi_{q}(\frac{1-t}{2}),
\displaystyle\omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)
\displaystyle:=\max_{\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)]}\omega(\beta),
\displaystyle\phi_{q}(s)
\displaystyle:=\frac{\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}(s)}{s}=\begin{cases}\frac{s\ln_{q}s+(1-s)\ln_{q}(1-s)}{s},&s\in(0,1]\\
\frac{-q}{q-1},&s=0\end{cases}.
The proof of this theorem is
similar to that of Theorem 5.2, and is provided in Appendix
G. Specifically, Lemma E.1 and the proof steps of Theorem 5.2 given in Section E hold verbatim with the substitutions \phi\leftarrow\phi_{q},\ln\leftarrow\ln_{q},\omega^{*}\leftarrow\omega_{q}^{*},\epsilon^{*}\leftarrow\epsilon_{q}^{*}. Similarly to the case q=1, in our proof, the last two constraints in (32) have been discarded, but numerical results indicate that this simplified bound retains full optimality for the specific purposes of this paper.
By this theorem, if for a given \rho, the maximum at the RHS of
(49) is no larger than \mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]=\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\frac{1+\rho}{2}),
then dictator functions are globally optimal in maximizing the q-stability
over all balanced Boolean functions. Since given \rho, if dictator
functions maximize the q-stability for some q\in[1,2), then dictator
functions maximize the \hat{q}-stability for any \hat{q}\in[q,2);
see [3, 34]. So, Theorem 5.5
in fact implies that for any \rho\in[0,0.914], dictator functions
maximize the q-stability for any q\in(1,2). Here, we only need focus
on the case of \rho\in[0.914,1].
Corollary 5.8.
Given q\in(1,2) and \rho\in(0,1), if
\displaystyle 1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)-(1-2\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho))(2-\rho^{2})
\displaystyle\geq 0,
(50)
\displaystyle\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in[0,1]\end{subarray}}\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)\right)\phi_{q}(\frac{1-t}{2})-\left(1+t-\rho^{2}\right)\phi_{q}(\frac{1-\rho}{2})\,
\displaystyle\leq 0,
(51)
then
\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
(52)
for all balanced Boolean functions f. In particular, given q\in(1,2),
if
\displaystyle\min_{\rho\in[0.914,1]}1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{0}-(1-2\epsilon_{0})(2-\rho^{2})
\displaystyle\geq 0,
(53)
\displaystyle\max_{\rho\in[0.914,1]}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in[0,1]\end{subarray}}\chi_{q}(\rho,t)\,
\displaystyle\leq 0,
(54)
where the function \chi_{q} is given by
\chi_{q}(\rho,t):=\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{0}\right)\phi_{q}(\frac{1-t}{2})-\left(1+t-\rho^{2}\right)\phi_{q}(\frac{1-\rho}{2}),
\epsilon_{0} is a number such that \epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)\geq\epsilon_{0},\forall\rho\in[0.914,1], and \omega_{0} is a number such that \omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)\leq\omega_{0},\forall\rho\in[0.914,1], then for all \rho\in[0.914,1], \mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
for all balanced Boolean functions f.
Remark 5.9.
Note that t\in[0,1]\mapsto\chi_{q}(\rho,t)
is concave, and hence the optimal t attaining the maximum in (54)
is the unique solution t_{q,\rho}\in(0,1) to the equation
-\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\rho-4\rho^{2}\omega_{0}\right)\chi_{q}^{\prime}(\frac{1-t}{2})-\chi_{q}(\frac{1-\rho}{2})=0.
(55)
The proof is similar to that of Corollary 5.3. It is straightforward to see that \eta_{q,2}(t)\leq\eta_{q,1}(t),\forall t\in[0,1] (defined in Theorem 5.7) if (50) holds.
If we can further show \eta_{q,1}(t)\leq\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}(\frac{1+\rho}{2}),\forall t\in[0,1],
or equivalently, the condition in (51),
then by Theorem 5.7, (52) holds for all
balanced Boolean functions f. Since \phi_{q} is negative,
the second statement follows obviously.
∎In the following, we analytically verify (53) and numerically verify (54) for q=1.36.
For q=1.36, we observe that for all \rho\in[0,1],
\epsilon_{q}^{*}(\rho)\geq\epsilon_{0}:=\epsilon_{q}^{*}(1)=0.188324...
(see Fig. 5), and for all \rho\in[0,1],
\omega_{q}^{*}(\rho)\leq\omega_{0}:=\max_{\beta\in[0,\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon_{q}^{*}(1)]}\omega(\beta)=\omega(\beta_{0})=0.193026...
where \beta_{0}=0.175661... Note that the objective function in (53) is a quadratic polynomial. We hence easily prove that the inequality in (53) holds in this case. On the other hand, using Matlab, we numerically verify
that for q=1.36,
\max_{\rho\in[0.914,1]}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}t\in[0,1]\end{subarray}}\chi_{q}(\rho,t)=-0.00169063...<0,
(56)
with the maximum attained at \rho=1 and t=0.858686...
Hence, for all 0.914\leq\rho\leq 1, dictator functions maximize the
q-stability with q=1.36 over all balanced Boolean functions.
Combining it with Theorem 5.6,
we conclude that for all \rho\in[0,1], dictator functions maximize
the q-stability with q=1.36 (and hence for all q\in[1.36,2))
over all balanced Boolean functions.
Fig 5: The plot of the function \epsilon_{q}^{*}
with q=1.36.
We employ a computer-assisted approach to rigorously verify the numerical observation stated above. The proof of the following theorem follows an argument nearly identical to that of Theorem 5.5; the complete derivation is provided in Appendix H.
Theorem 5.10.
The optimal value of (56) for \Phi=\Phi_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}
with q=1.36 is negative. In other words, for any \rho\in[0,1]
and q\in[1.36,2), it holds that \mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f]\leq\mathbf{Stab}_{q}^{\mathrm{sym}}[f_{\mathrm{d}}]
for all balanced Boolean functions f.
Remark 5.11.
It is already known [34, 24] that for q\in[2,5],
dictator functions maximize the symmetric q-stability over all
balanced Boolean functions. So, combining it with this theorem, we
know that for q\in[1.36,5], dictator functions maximize the symmetric
q-stability.
Li and Médard conjectured that dictator functions maximize the symmetric
q-stability for all q\in(1,2). The theorem above implies that
the Li–Médard conjecture is true for all q\in[1.36,2). Furthermore, it was observed that dictator functions maximizing the \hat{q}-stability
for some \hat{q}\in(0,2) implies dictator functions maximizing the q-stability
for all q\in[\hat{q},2) [3]. So, Theorem 5.6
implies that the Li–Médard conjecture is also true for q\in(1,1.36)
and \rho\in[0,0.914].
Theorem 5.12 (Restatement of Theorem 1.6).
The (symmetrized) Li–Médard conjecture is
true for all q\in[1.36,2) and \rho\in[0,1], and also true for all q\in(1,1.36) and \rho\in[0,0.914].
The Li–Médard conjecture is still open for the case of q\in(1,1.36)
and \rho\in(0.914,1). The bound here for q\in[1.36,2) is obtained
from Corollary 5.8. In fact, for q\in(1,1.36),
we numerically evaluate our bound in Corollary 5.8
and find a region of (q,\rho) for which dictator functions maximize
the q-stability (i.e., for which the Li–Médard conjecture is
true). We plot this region in Fig. 1.
5.3 q-Stability with 0<q<1
It is natural to further investigate whether dictator functions maximize
q-stability for 0<q<1. In this subsection, we connect q-stability of a
Boolean function with the edge-boundary of its support. Via this connection, we observe that
dictator functions are not extremizers anymore for 0<q<1/2, but we conjecture that
they are indeed extremizers for 1/2\leq q<1.
Let \mathbf{X} be a random vector
uniformly distributed on the discrete cube \{\pm 1\}^{n}. Let \mathbf{Y}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}
be the random vector obtained by independently changing the sign of
each component of \mathbf{X} with the same probability \frac{1-\rho}{2}.
Let A be the support of f. Then,
\displaystyle T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})
\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{Y}\in A|\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\mathbf{y}\in A}\left(\frac{1+\rho}{2}\right)^{n-d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})}\left(\frac{1-\rho}{2}\right)^{d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})},
where d(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{x})=|\{i\in[n]:y_{i}\neq x_{i}\}| is
the Hamming distance between \mathbf{x} and \mathbf{y}.
Lemma 5.13.
Let f:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\} be any Boolean
function with support A. Then, the following hold.
1.
Denote t=(\frac{1-\rho}{2})^{q}, i.e., \rho=1-2t^{1/q}. It holds
that for 0<q<1,
\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}f)^{q}]\big|_{t=0}
\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[h_{A^{c}}^{q}],
where for B\subset\{\pm 1\}^{n}, h_{B}:\{\pm 1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}
is defined by h_{B}(\mathbf{x}) equaling the number of edges joining
\mathbf{x} with a vertex in B^{c} if \mathbf{x}\in B, and
h_{B}(\mathbf{x})=0 if \mathbf{x}\in B^{c}.
2.
Denote t=\rho^{2}, i.e., \rho=\sqrt{t}. It holds that for 0<q<1,
\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}f)^{q}]\big|_{t=0}
\displaystyle=\frac{q(q-1)}{2}\alpha^{q-2}\mathbf{W}_{1}[f],
(57)
where \alpha=\mathbb{E}[f] is the mean of f and \mathbf{W}_{1}[f]=\sum_{|S|=1}\hat{f}_{S}^{2}
is the first-level Fourier weight of f with \hat{f}_{S},S\subseteq[n]
denoting the Fourier coefficients of f.
Remark 5.14.
In contrast, for q>1, it is known [22] that
\displaystyle\partial_{\rho}\mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}f)^{q}]\big|_{\rho=1}
\displaystyle=q\mathbb{E}[h_{A}],
where \mathbb{E}[h_{A}]=\mathbb{E}[h_{A^{c}}] is the classic edge-boundary
of A (or A^{c}) normalized by 2^{n}. Note that \mathbb{E}[h_{A^{c}}^{q}]
is a variant of edge-boundary of A^{c} which reduces to the edge-boundary
for q=1 and reduces to the vertex-boundary for q=0. This quantity
has attracted considerable attention from the probability community
and discrete analysis community [31, 5, 17, 4, 11].
Statement 1: Observe that
\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbb{E}[(T_{\rho}f)^{q}]
\displaystyle=\frac{q}{2^{n}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\left(T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\right)^{q-1}\partial_{t}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})
\displaystyle=\frac{q}{2^{n}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\left(T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\right)^{q-1}\left(\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1-2t^{1/q}}\right)\left(\frac{-2}{q}t^{1/q-1}\right)
\displaystyle=\frac{-1}{2^{n-1}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\left(T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\right)^{q-1}\left(\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1-2t^{1/q}}\right)t^{1/q-1}
\displaystyle=\frac{-1}{2^{n-1}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\left(\frac{T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})}{t^{1/q}}\right)^{q-1}\left(\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1-2t^{1/q}}\right)
\displaystyle\to\frac{-1}{2^{n-1}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\lim_{\rho\to 1}\left(\frac{2T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})}{1-\rho}\right)^{q-1}\left(\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1}\right)
\displaystyle=\frac{-1}{2^{n-1}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}}\left(\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1}\right)\times\begin{cases}0,&\mathbf{x}\in A\\
\left(-2\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1}\right)^{q-1},&\mathbf{x}\in A^{c}\end{cases}
\displaystyle=\frac{2^{q-1}}{2^{n-1}}\sum_{\mathbf{x}\in A^{c}}\left(-\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})\big|_{\rho=1}\right)^{q}.
For \mathbf{x}\in A^{c},
\displaystyle\partial_{\rho}T_{\rho}f(\mathbf{x})
